title: The road to Chitrakuta
hookLine: a sage gives directions the old way, and every river on the road becomes a prayer
carry: a tirtha is a holy crossing

lines: A RIVER, A TREE, A GROVE.
cards: Before maps on phones, directions were stories. Go past the old mill, turn at the big oak, and when you see the water tower, you're nearly there.
Bharadvaja gives Rama directions like that the next morning: a river to cross, a tree to look for, a grove to walk through, and then a mountain.
He's sending them to the place where they'll make their first home in exile, and he describes it with love.

teach.b: There's a mountain, Bharadvaja says, about ten kroshas from here, called Chitrakuta. Sages live there. Peacocks call on its slopes, monkeys play in the trees, and there's fruit and honey everywhere.
Follow the Yamuna until you find a crossing. Build a raft, and cross.

teach.h: A PRAYER AT THE DARK BANYAN.
teach.b: On the other side you'll find a great banyan with dark leaves, called Shyama, the dark one. People pray there. Walk on past it to a grove, and the road to the mountain.
At the river, Rama and Lakshmana tie bamboo and dry wood together with creepers, and Lakshmana builds Sita a little seat of branches.
In the middle of the Yamuna, as on the Ganga, Sita folds her hands and speaks to the river, asking for her husband's safe return and vowing offerings when they come home.
On the far bank she bows to the dark banyan and prays again, for Rama, for Lakshmana, for the day they'll see their mothers. Every crossing gets a prayer. Hindus have a word for that: tirtha.

teach.h: TIRTHA: A FORD, A HOLY PLACE.
teach.b: It first meant a ford, a place to cross a river, and it came to mean a holy place, where, as many teachers put it, you cross over from the ordinary toward God.
Prayaga, where they started, is one of the greatest tirthas, and a pilgrimage is a tirtha yatra, a journey of holy crossings.
Sita's prayer at the tree has a living echo too: on the day called Vat Savitri, many Hindu women worship the banyan for their husbands' long lives.

how: In the text, Sita honors the Yamuna as she honored the Ganga; Hindus still go on tirtha yatra to holy rivers, and on Vat Savitri many women worship the banyan for their husbands' long lives.

o: the sage who sends the exiles to Chitrakuta
the boatman who ferries the exiles over the Yamuna
the hermit who builds the exiles a hut of leaves

games.q: the sage's directions — tap the pairs.
p: a mountain of peacocks and honey
bamboo and wood tied with creepers
a ford, then a holy place

s: the exiles cross the Yamuna by a ferry
they build a raft themselves from bamboo and wood.
Sita prays to the Yamuna, as she did to the Ganga
and again at the dark banyan tree.
tirtha first meant a ford, a place to cross a river
it came to mean a holy place: where you cross over toward God.

games.q: you're Sita, on a raft in the middle of the Yamuna, the second great river of your exile. what do you do?
o: pray to the river for a safe return.
ask to go back to Bharadvaja.
games.why: she folds her hands and prays to the Yamuna, and again at the banyan: every crossing a tirtha.

practice: Picture the route you take most days, and three landmarks along it: a bridge, a corner, a tree. Walk it slowly in your mind, and at each one pause for a full breath, as if it were a tirtha.
If you pray, fold your hands there in your mind, as Sita did. Then rest.

wordCard.voice: Bharadvaja, part two. The sage sends the exiles to Chitrakuta, and Sita turns a raft, a river and a dark banyan into a chain of tirthas.

orig.note: Sanskrit yamunā: the river Yamuna, honored as a goddess; the exiles cross it by raft.

carryVoice: Your line: a tirtha is a holy crossing. The three exiles are almost home now. See you tomorrow.
